Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) officers detained Airida Gould, a Lithuanian national married to a U.S. Army veteran for over a decade, during a green card interview in May, her husband, Mark Gould, told Newsweek. The Chicago-area woman had a prior removal order from 2009. Her husband told Newsweek on Tuesday night that his wife "is being deported this evening from Chicago O'Hare [Airport]." In an update Wednesday night he said he was unable to see her before she was deported to Lithuania. Read More on U.S. A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson told Newsweek that Gould entered the U.S. "in June 2000 on a visa that would allow her to stay in the country until December 2009. In violation of our nation’s laws, she overstayed her visa. An immigration judge ordered her removed in August 2009." Gould's case comes amid reports of increased arrests at immigration appointments, including green card interviews and mandatory check-ins, as the Trump administration intensifies enforcement efforts. Newsweek reached out to Gould’s lawyer for comment via email. ... What To Know Mark Gould, a 61-year-old Army veteran, said he accompanied his wife to a U.S. government building on May 14 for an immigration appointment in what they believed was their “final step” in the green card process, according to a GoFundMe campaign he created following her detention. “That morning, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services approved our marriage petition, officially confirming what we have known since the day we married: ours is a real marriage, a real family, and Airida belongs here,” he wrote. When asked for comment and confirmation, USCIS directed Newsweek to the DHS. A DHS spokesperson told Newsweek that "The filing or approval of a Form I-130, Petition for Alien Relative petition does not grant any immigration status or benefit." Gould continued, “Hours later, at that same appointment, in that same building, my wife was handcuffed and taken away by ICE.” Airida Gould was in ICE custody until Tuesday, according to the agency's online detainee locator, which lists her as Airida Kesiliene and places her at the Broadview Service Staging Area in Illinois. The Broadview facility has previously been at the center of anti-ICE demonstrations. In September 2025, protesters gathered repeatedly outside the processing center to oppose the Trump administration's immigration enforcement operations, with some demonstrations ending in clashes between federal agents and activists. However, an ABC7 report said Gould was being held at a detention facility in Kentucky after being transferred from Illinois and Indiana. As of Thursday, the ICE detainee tracker does not show Gould in the system. Her husband told Newsweek on Wednesday she was transferred back to Broadview on Tuesday hours ahead of her deportation flight. She had described her prior detention conditions to ABC7 , saying, "I think people taking care better for their cats and dogs. That bad, that place definitely probably has to be closed." She told the outlet that at her new facility, she gets fresh air for one hour, three times a week. A DHS spokesperson told Newsweek, "All detainees are provided with proper meals, water, medical treatment, and have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers. ICE has higher detention standards than most U.S. prisons that hold actual U.S. citizens." The statement continued, "It is a longstanding practice to provide comprehensive medical care from the moment an alien enters ICE custody. This includes medical, dental, and mental health services as available, and access to medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care. This is the best healthcare than many aliens have received in their entire lives." ... In a video posted Tuesday to the Facebook page Bring Airida Home , which was created by her husband, said she was being deported to Europe. In an email to Newsweek , he provided her deportation flight information, which showed a flight to Warsaw, Poland and then a connecting flight to Vilnius, Lithuania. She arrived at 4:30 pm local time on Wednesday, he said. From there she went to her hometown of Kailpeda. He captioned the video, "After 66 days in captivity, ICE allowed me to give Airida some cash, cards and carry on. Of course when I asked to see her and give her a hug it was denied. Took everything in me not to get arrested. I will NEVER, Forget and NEVER forgive these monsters. Airida is leaving tonight, no details provided." While Gould's family acknowledges she was subject to a 2009 removal order, her husband wrote in a GoFundMe campaign that the order was issued after she arrived late to a court hearing because of road construction. "The matter was never heard on its merits," he wrote. Gould is represented by former Chicago immigration court Judge Carla Espinoza Grcic. Her legal team has filed an Emergency Motion to Reopen with the Board of Immigration Appeals. Related Story ICE to Require Body Cameras During Vehicle Stops After Fatal Encounters Green Card Marriages Marriage to a U.S. citizen remains a common route to obtaining a green card. But immigration attorneys and advocates say the Trump administration has stepped up enforcement and vetting involving citizens' spouses, while administration officials argue they are enforcing laws that were not adequately applied under previous administrations. Marriage-based green cards allow foreign-born spouses of U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents to obtain permanent residency in the United States. Spouses of U.S. citizens are classified as "immediate relatives," making them exempt from annual visa caps. Officials review multiple factors to confirm the legitimacy of a marriage , including shared living arrangements, joint financial responsibilities, and other evidence that the couple maintains a life together. Couples who live apart, submit inconsistent documentation, or appear to have entered the marriage for immigration purposes may face additional scrutiny, longer processing times, or outright denial of their application. DHS data show that about 343,000 spouses of U.S. citizens obtained lawful permanent residence in fiscal year 2024, accounting for about half the green cards issued to "immediate relatives of U.S. citizens." Overall, about 1.36 million people became lawful permanent residents across all admission classes that year. Who Is Airida Gould? Gould came to the United States in 2000 and has three U.S.-born children, Lucas, 23, Jamie, 20, and Nojus, 17, her husband wrote in the GoFundMe. Court records reviewed by Newsweek show a 2017 traffic citation for following another vehicle too closely. Gould, 53, worked as a licensed massage therapist at the same business, Libertyville Massage Therapy, for two decades. The business posted about Gould on their Instagram page in June, writing, “Airida was taken into custody due to a decades-old court order related to a missed hearing. She is being held in an out-of-state detention facility while her case moves through the immigration process.” The business asked customers to sign a petition on her behalf. Read more Former Strictly Come Dancing stars James and Ola Jordan have spoken out about the “difficult personal challenges” that led to their split. It was announced on Saturday that the couple, who have been married since 2003 and share a six-year-old daughter named Ella, are “taking some time apart”. Their manager, Vickie White, said that the pair “began a trial separation some time ago”. The Jordans have now shared a joint statement, posted across both of their Instagram pages. “We have always tried to be open and honest with the people who have supported us over the years and we feel it’s only right that this update comes from us,” they said. “At the moment we’re taking some time apart as we work through very difficult personal challenges.” open image in gallery Ola and James Jordan at Royal Ascot in 2018 ( Getty Images for Ascot ) The statement said that James “moved out of the family home some time ago”, and explained that their separation “wasn’t an easy decision”. James, 48, and Ola, 43, are professional ballroom dancers and choreographers best known for their roles on Strictly. The pair became household names after joining the show in 2006. James featured on the show until 2013, partnering with stars such as Pamela Stephenson , Alex Jones, Denise Van Outen and Vanessa Feltz. Ola competed on Strictly until 2015, where she danced with celebrities including DJ Spoony, Sid Owen, Steve Backshall and Iwan Thomas. The Polish-born dancer also won the Glitterball trophy in 2009, partnered with TV personality Chris Hollins. open image in gallery Ola and James have been together for 26 years and share a young daughter ( Getty ) James and Ola conceived Ella through IVF, and she was born in 2020 following a widely publicised three-year fertility struggle. Their statement continued: “Our absolute priority, now and always, is our beautiful daughter Ella. She’s at the centre of everything we do. “We are committed to co-parenting her with all the love, care and stability she deserves.” It also discussed James’ mental wellbeing, saying he “hasn’t been in a good place for quite some time”. “I’ve been struggling more than I’ve let people see and I’m taking the time I need to focus on getting myself to a healthier place, both for myself and for Ella,” it added. The statement continued: “Neither of us is in a good place right now. “We’re both doing our best to navigate one of the hardest chapters of our lives and we ask that people remember there are real people and real emotions behind every headline, every comment and every post. “We don’t know exactly what the future holds. For now, we’re taking things one day at a time, doing what we both believe is best for ourselves, our family, and most importantly Ella.” The message concluded by thanking their followers, fans and supporters for “the love, kindness and concern” that they have shown. The couple also asked for “kindness, empathy and a little privacy as we work through this as a family”. https://theweek.com/edition/theweekus-ev.text: Livestreaming an execution: cruelty or added deterrent? Nearly a century after holding its last public execution, the U.S. government this month announced plans to broadcast the December execution of Nidal Hasan, a former army officer convicted for the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood. Not only will he be killed by firing squad, said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, but the government intends to “make sure people are able to watch it, that it’s public.” Unsurprisingly, the plans to federally livestream a shooting death have prompted both massive condemnation and pockets of support from many in President Donald Trump’s MAGA coalition. ‘Public and brutal, not private and medicalized’ Livestreaming Hasan’s death is “excellent,” said Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) on X. A public execution is “what this terrorist deserves.” Critics simply don’t have to watch the killing “if they don’t choose to,” said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on CBS News’ “Face The Nation with Margaret Brennan” this weekend. Executions should be “public and brutal, not private and medicalized,” said defense tech executive and newly named Pentagon consultant Palmer Luckey on X. “You live by the sword, you die by the sword,” said retired Staff Sgt. Alonzo Lunsford, who survived Hasan’s attack, to NBC News. “He needs to go out by firing squad.” But while Lunsford “endorses livestreaming the event,” said the outlet, he also expressed concern over children seeing Hasan’s death. ‘Beyond disgusting’ The broad American public is “overwhelmingly against the Pentagon’s decision,” said Fox News. Those who spoke with the network “blasted the broadcast as ‘a shame’ and ‘just weird.’” Although Hasan “should face the death penalty,” livestreaming his killing is “beyond disgusting,” said retiring North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis on X. Any Catholic service members detailed to Hasan’s firing squad should “request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church,” said Archbishop for the Military Services Timothy P. Broglio in a statement. Notably, Trump has “privately shared misgivings” about livestreaming the execution, said Axios. He “didn’t sound particularly enthusiastic” about the broadcast, said one confidante to the outlet. “That’s why he’s calling around, doing the Trump thing, asking people what they think.” QUOTE OF THE DAY ‘You don’t get to take a man from his family. You don’t get to take his very life, his whole future from him, and just walk away from it. Especially when that man is Tupac Shakur.’ Judge Carli Kierny speaking to Duane “Keffe D” Davis before sentencing him to a minimum of 40 years in prison for first-degree murder and use of a deadly weapon in the 1996 shooting of Tupac Shakur. The 63-year-old Davis said he will appeal the guilty verdict. today’s big question Can a Democrat win the Texas governor’s race? James Talarico is not the only Democrat with a shot at winning an election in Texas. Polls show challenger Gina Hinojosa ( pictured above ), spurred on by Latino voters and the data center backlash, is running neck and neck with longtime GOP incumbent Greg Abbott in the governor’s race. What did the commentators say? Polls have the Hinojosa-Abbott race “statistically tied” heading into the final weeks, said The Center Square. It’s a startling turn for Abbott, who’s seeking a fourth term. He has never lost a statewide election “by less than 11 points,” said Slate. But some rural voters are defecting over Abbott’s “past support for data centers,” and Lone Star Latino voters are turning against the GOP because of the “president’s handling of the economy and mass deportations,” said NBC News. Hinojosa is “perhaps the most serious electoral challenger” Abbott has faced, said the Houston Chronicle. The Democrat has sharpened a “populist message” that asks voters to “set aside the culture wars” in favor of policies and politicians that help them “make ends meet.” The message arrives amid voter anger over “rising prices and seemingly unchecked growth of Big Tech.” Democrats have long dreamed of a “blue Texas,” said Nicole Russell at USA Today. Nonetheless, the Lone Star State is “one of the top places Americans move” because it has no income tax and is affordable. All that is made possible by “embracing conservative values.” Voters will not want to “upend that way of life” by electing a Democrat. What next? Polls in previous elections have given Texas Democrats “reason to hope for an upset” only to end in disappointment, said The Washington Post. Hinojosa still faces an uphill climb. A Democrat has not been in the Texas governor's mansion since Ann Richards in 1990. But national Democrats are “stepping up” their support for Hinojosa, said CBS News. The Democratic Governors Association and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker are both putting “at least $1 million” toward her election. Statistic of the day 5 million: The approximate number of Americans who have lost SNAP benefits since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed in 2025 — a 13% drop year-over-year, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Arizona has had the largest loss so far at 50%. in the spotlight Drones and drills: why Lithuania feels vulnerable Following his country’s largest airport was forced to close due to a suspected drone attack thought to have originated in Belarus, the prime minister of Lithuania has called for a NATO plan to respond to Russia’s hybrid warfare. As such “incidents spread beyond Europe’s eastern flank,” said Politico, he warns that Moscow is prepared to test the alliance. Forced shelter Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. A drone that violated Lithuanian airspace was shot down in September, following similar incidents in Latvia and Estonia. In May, residents in Vilnius were “forced to take shelter” across the capital after a drone alert was “triggered,” briefly grounding flights and rail travel, said the BBC. Lithuania, a “staunch supporter” of Ukraine, shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a “key Russian ally,” said the outlet. Sinkevicius warns that a Russian victory in Ukraine would probably push Moscow to look for “other directions.” Achilles’ heel A “tranquil corner” of Lithuania is now a “tinderbox that could help trigger World War III,” said The Sun. The gap is “one of the most volatile points on the world map,” said former U.S. Army General Ben Hodges, per the outlet. Spanning 40 miles as the crow flies, the Suwalki Gap is a corridor of land that runs along the Polish-Lithuanian border connects the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad to Belarus. Called the “most dangerous place on Earth,” the gap has long been viewed as the Achilles’ heel of NATO’s eastern defenses, because Russia could seize it relatively easily by launching a pincer assault between Kaliningrad in the northwest and Belarus in the southeast, said Der Stern. The creation of such a land bridge would effectively isolate the Baltic states of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, all of which are NATO members, from the EU. Lithuania has been “holding military drills and rehearsing wartime evacuation plans,” said The Sun. It allocated almost $5.6 billion to defense this year — 5.38% of its GDP, “dwarfing the U.K. spend of just 2.6%.” Good day 🐴 … for New York horses. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has reached a deal to ban horse-drawn carriages, popular in Central Park, beginning in 2028, according to Politico. Animal welfare activists have long fought to end their use, which has been a city staple for 150 years. Bad day 🍻 … for British pubs. Every day, a bar in the U.K. closes, according to the British Beer and Pub Association. In the first nine months of 2026, 295 were permanently shuttered, and the total is expected to reach at least 360 by the end of the year. Picture of the day ‘The Meeting Place’ A young bull elephant sprays zebras at a watering hole in Kenya’s Chyulu Hills. This photograph by the U.K.’s James Lewin has topped the Animals in their Environment category of the Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition. James Lewin / Wildlife Photographer of the Year Puzzles Daily sudoku Challenge yourself with The Week’s daily sudoku, part of our puzzles section, which also includes guess the number Play here The Week recommends A book for cooking like a Cajun “My most cherished food memories involve two ingredients: rice and pork,” said chef Donald Link in his book, “Real Cajun: Rustic Home Cooking.” It’s a common refrain for people raised in the prairies and bayous of southern Louisiana. The rice is there in the region’s popular eggplant dressing, dirty rice with chicken livers, and crawfish pies. Pork appears as cracklins, those deep-fried nubbins of seasoned pork belly, and in all manner of Deep South charcuterie. Rice and pork even tango together in the legendary sausage called boudin. Link is the owner of a handful of restaurants in New Orleans, and this cookbook takes you on a tour of the tastes of his homeland. Two foundational ingredients No two boudins are alike, but they are “all good,” said Link in his book. He stars both pork shoulder and liver, plus two types of fresh chiles, a glut of spices and, of course, white rice. Lima beans appear in a stew alongside smoked sausage, and a suave pork roast is served over, yes, rice. Even chicken thighs are stuffed with sausage. Pork is ubiquitous, and rice nearly as much, appearing in a gratin with zucchini, a soup with chicken, and a fritter known as calas. And beyond Freshness and fiber are everywhere across “Real Cajun.” Tender lettuces are slicked with a scallion-buttermilk dressing, and tomatoes bring a lush tang to stewed okra. A sweet finish is obligatory. So there are recipes for satsuma-buttermilk pie, blueberry cobbler, and a staple of Link’s youth, lemon meringue pie. Man cannot live on rice and pork alone. Poll watch A fifth of Americans (20%) are more interested in owning nice things now than they were a decade ago, according to an Economist/YouGov survey of 1,403 adults. For almost half (48%), their interest level hasn’t changed, while nearly a third (32%) are less interested. INSTANT OPINION Today’s best commentary ‘Ilhan Omar raid is Trump’s playbook. Stop acting surprised.’ Sara Pequeño at USA Today The public humiliation of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar is “not an outlier” for Trump — it’s the “point of his presidency,” says Sara Pequeño. It has become the “Republican way of politics.” But if anything, the president has “given her something else to run on.” Her resilience in the face of his administration’s pointed attack will “endear her to her community,” especially “fellow immigrants who see themselves in her.” It’s a “miscalculation” that will “only ensure a bigger election blue wave come November.” ‘The US can’t ignore the horrors of forced organ harvesting’ Robert George at The Washington Post Organ donation can be a “lifesaving gift of modern medicine,” but it must never be an “occasion of injustice or an assault on the sanctity of human life,” says Robert George. The provisions of the Stop Forced Organ Harvesting Act — “imposing sanctions, asset freezes, visa bans and passport revocations on those complicit” — would “make clear” that the U.S. opposes organ theft “wherever it occurs.” It should wait for passage, “without any watering down of its provisions,” no longer. ‘Celebrities who shill for sports betting are the modern Marlboro Men’ Myron Levin at the Los Angeles Times Celebrity endorsers present sports betting as “cool and exciting entertainment” without a “whiff of danger,” says Myron Levin. There’s no mention of the risk, such as “financial loss, psychological harm and family disruption,” that “already afflicts millions of Americans.” While online gambling, like smoking, has “grown wildly popular,” its “long-term societal impacts” are “still being learned.” One day, when we “weigh the damage,” we may “look back on the celebrity hype” with a “similar sense of surprise and disdain.” WORD OF THE DAY techno-optimism The belief that technology will solve global problems like climate change. In a survey of more than 9,000 scientists in 115 countries, 27% of those who identify as techno-optimists are 23% less likely to participate in climate action than their tech-skeptic peers, according to the London School of Economics.
